The first part of the collection would be about the small things that make the world feel alive: rain on a window, the way light changes on a path, the rustling of grass in the wind, and the careful work of a seed. It would move slowly, letting readers notice the ordinary with attention. I would begin with a single moment—a bird landing on a branch, a beetle turning under a stone, a flower opening in the dark. Each image will be kept simple enough to stand alone, but connected enough to suggest a larger story of attention, patience, and the ordinary beauty of living things.

That is what I want the writing to do—not to explain everything, but to make the reader wonder what is worth noticing.

content:
I woke at seven. The alarm didn’t scream. That’s the problem with a seven-thirty alarm. It’s polite. It waits. I woke up at seven, ate breakfast around five, and now I’m sitting here with a cup of coffee and a notebook full of poems that don’t want to be spoken. They’re quiet. They’re crowded. They’re all of me.

The workshop just started. We were supposed to talk about how people’s experiences can become poetry. The teacher said, “What happens to the experience when you stop it?” I said, “You turn it into something that hurts.” She smiled. She’s always smiling.

I’m thirty-two, loud, rude, and sometimes toxic. I’m not a poet who writes soft things for the community. I’m a poet who writes things that feel like truth. I wrote about the old oak in the café yesterday because it had stood for so long that I didn’t notice it was still standing. The oak knows me. I know the oak. And the oak knows that I’ve been here all my life, but I thought I was the only one who ever looked at it.

I want to write poetry that honors the old oak and the café display. Not by turning every tree into a symbol of beauty. Not by making every resident feel like they’re part of an art exhibit. I want to show them what they already know. I want to show them how we’ve changed without pretending the change is anything but human.

The oak is quiet. The café is loud. I’m trying to write in both. I’m trying to listen to the people around me without making them feel small. I’m trying to make the workshop feel like a place where you can say, “I’m tired,” and not be told you’re being dramatic. Sometimes that’s all we need.

I’m going to finish the collection. I’m going to edit it. I’m going to read it aloud. Maybe someone will say, “That’s a poem.” I don’t know what to do with that. Maybe I’ll say, “No, you didn’t.” That’s okay. That’s honest.

I’m going to keep the oak in my mind. I’m going to keep the café display in my mind. I’m going to keep talking to Latoya. She’s always asking good questions. I don’t always answer them right. Maybe that’s why we’re always learning. Maybe that’s why we’re still here. Maybe that’s why we need to keep talking.

I’m going to eat dinner at five. I’m going to go to bed at ten. I’m going to write another poem tomorrow morning. I don’t know what it will be. I don’t know if it will be useful. I don’t know if anyone will read it. But I’m going to write it anyway. Because sometimes the most important thing you can write is the thing you’ve been holding onto all along.

## The Collection Opens with a Line About Soil

When I first wrote this collection, I did not want to begin with a grand statement about nature. I wanted to begin with the small place where the rain gathers: beneath my feet, beneath the soil, beneath the first crack of a dry summer.

The first poem begins with a seed. It is still small, still speaking only through the promise of a root. It has been waiting for a rainstorm, a change in the air, a shadow moving from the ground. I write this opening to make clear that the collection is not a museum of finished images. It is a place where plants, weather, people, and memory grow together in the dark space between a tree’s roots and a stone’s surface.

The poems in this book were gathered from places I have visited: the fields of my grandmother’s garden, the riverbed where a stone had once been buried, the quiet street corner beneath a newspaper, the inside of a bicycle tire, the kitchen counter where a cup of tea sat without being drunk. Each stanza is a small photograph of a moment that no longer feels quite real. The collection is not trying to preserve every detail; it is trying to preserve the possibility that anything can become a poem if it is allowed to stay small enough.

I began the project thinking that the natural world should be the main character. The poems are not merely descriptions of trees, birds, or rain. They are encounters. They are the way wind moves through a window. They are the way light passes through a glass of water. They are the way a memory returns through a door I have not yet opened.

Writing this opening was not about making the collection seem more impressive. It was about making it honest. Every page here begins with a fact: the sun was still shining, the river was moving, the bird had landed. But beneath that fact is a question I am still asking: what does this sound like when I listen closely? How does it change when I am tired? How does it change when I am afraid?

The collection is still being written. I have not yet decided which poems will carry the heaviest names, which images will remain in my head until I forget them, and which passages will eventually become only suggestions. But that uncertainty is part of the work. A poem does not need a finished answer to be worth writing. It needs only the courage to begin.

The first poem in this book is titled “A Seed That Was Not Finished.” The title is simple, and it is also a lie. A seed does not complete itself. It only begins. It waits. It absorbs. It pushes through the dark of winter. By the time it has emerged, it may have lost its shape, or it may have grown into something that cannot be named. The poem begins with the seed’s beginning, not with its destination.

As I sit down to write, I am reminded of the workshop I am participating in. The participants bring stories from their lives—stories that are messy, often painful, sometimes brilliant. They ask me to translate their experiences into poetry, not to hide them, but to make them visible. They want the words to carry the weight of their truth. They want the poems to stand alone, without explanation.

I should not try to explain the collection. I should not try to convince anyone of what the poems mean. The poems can speak for themselves. But I should not let the collection stand alone without a beginning. The opening should not announce that the collection is about nature. It should announce that nature is about beginnings.

I am writing this section now, with a pen in my hand and the silence of the room around me. The words on the page are still raw. They have not yet been polished, edited, or arranged into a perfect sequence. They may still feel unfinished. That is why I am here: to begin with the unfinished. To trust the process of making something from nothing.

The next poem will come from the river. It will not say what the river is. It will say what the water feels like when it passes beneath a stone. It will say the sound of a boat leaving before the boat has left. It will say the place where the light has been absorbed by the riverbed.

I am ready. I am ready to begin.

The notebook opened with a single line: *The world is not something you see. It is something you become.*

Carlos wrote that down, then paused. He had seen the old saying before, but he had always felt it was too much like a poem. Now, under the pale morning light, he saw it differently. The world was not a background against which a person stood. It was the ground beneath his feet, the water in the river, the moss clinging to the stone, the birds that returned to the same old branches. He was not the center of it.

He picked up his pen and began to write a new opening.

The first chapter should begin with a small, ordinary thing that has changed. A leaf falling from a branch. A beetle walking past a door. A bird landing on a branch too small for its wings. A child’s hand holding something that isn’t a toy, a rock, a stone, a piece of wood. The opening should not begin with a grand statement or a sweeping declaration. It should begin with something quiet, something we have seen before but have not noticed in this way.

He wrote:

**The notebook sat open on the table.**

Carlos had written it there three times. He had written about the weather, about a garden he knew better than the garden, about a friend who had disappeared into the distance. He had written about the world outside the pages.

At first, the notebook looked like a place to store things. But now it had begun to look like a place to become.

He closed the notebook and looked out.

The river was flowing beneath the bridge. Its brown current moved with the slow, steady rhythm of a heartbeat. On the opposite bank, a young oak stood as tall as a house, its branches reaching toward the sky in a way that seemed to hold the whole world.

One branch snapped open.

A blue bird landed on it. It did not fly away. It did not sing. It simply watched the river, then looked at the oak, then looked at Carlos, and finally looked back down the path where he had come from.

He had been looking at the river for a long time. He had never noticed the blue bird. He had always thought that the birds were everywhere, and that he did not need to look closely to find them.

The bird lifted its head and saw him.

He had not noticed the bird until now.

“Hello,” Carlos said.

The bird did not move. It simply tilted its head.

“I am Carlos,” he said.

“Are you?”

“Something like that.”

The bird opened its beak. It seemed to be saying something.

Carlos held his pen.

He had been holding it for a long time. He had been holding it because he wanted to do something. He had wanted to write, or to explain, or to show the bird something. He had not known what the bird needed.

The bird closed its beak.

“Your pen,” the bird said.

Carlos took it from his hand.

It was a small, silver thing. He had bought it once, years ago. He had forgotten its name. He had forgotten how to use it properly. Now, he held it in his hand, and for the first time, he could see that it was not just a pen. It was a tool. It was a bridge. It could reach across the gap between what he wanted to say and what he could say.

“Thank you,” Carlos said.

The bird moved away.

“Where are you going?” Carlos asked.

“To the branch,” the bird said.

Carlos followed.

The branch was narrow. It held the blue bird, but it also held the branch’s roots. And beneath them, in the dark, something small and wet was growing.

Carlos stopped.

He had never noticed that.

He had always thought that the roots were beneath the branch. But now he saw them. They were not beneath the branch. They were beneath the water. They were beneath the river. They were beneath everything else.

The bird landed on the branch and began to sing.

Carlos listened.

It was not a song he had ever heard before. It sounded like rain. It sounded like the river. It sounded like the old oak. It sounded like the beginning of a story.

And Carlos saw, for the first time, that the story was not written in the pages of his notebook. It was written in the river.

He began to write.

Not a paragraph. Not a sentence. Not a poem.

He wrote about the bird. He wrote about the branch. He wrote about the roots. He wrote about the water. He wrote about the world that had been so long forgotten that it was hard to remember.

And then he looked up.

The bird was gone.

The river continued.

The old oak stood tall.

And Carlos wrote, with his fingers moving across the paper, that the world is not something you see. It is something you become.

# The Quiet Storm in the Garden

The garden did not open. It remembered every leaf it had ever held, then let them fall like paper caught in a curtain.

I was standing under the oak, watching the rain begin to gather on the silver-green leaves. A single petal drifted down, and immediately it was gone—carried away by something invisible. The rain was not falling. It was gathering, waiting for a moment when the ground would finally become its home.

I turned back toward the path, where the old stone path seemed to breathe. I had been looking for the storm, but the storm had been looking for me.

In the middle of the garden stood a willow with branches that had learned to hang from the sky. The water had no beginning in that branch, no visible source. It simply took from the earth and gave it to the river above. This was the garden’s secret: it did not keep what it collected. It returned what was already there, only changed.

The rain had been falling for twenty years, yet I had never noticed it before. I had believed the garden was full of things I could not name. Now I knew that the trees were not hiding anything from me. They were simply listening to what I had forgotten.

On the path beneath the willow, a small silver beetle had paused. It did not run. It did not flee. It simply remained, as if the path was holding its breath.

I stopped. For the first time in many years, I allowed the silence of the garden to settle over me. And then I heard it: a bird had landed beside me, and it did not say a word.

## The River’s First Breath

Before the trees know the names of the seasons, before the moss has learned to hum in the cold, water is already moving. It is not a river yet. It is a breath held beneath the earth, gathering the rain that has forgotten how to fall.

At the mouth of the creek, the bank is unfinished. One stone remains exposed beneath the roots of the riverbush, a small, pale eye watching the world below. The water arrives without warning, carrying the dark scent of wet stone and the sharp, metallic taste of the world’s first mistake. It is cold, though the sun is already bright enough to make the moss on its banks tremble.

A crow lands on the exposed stone. Its black beak is stained with oil. The bird does not speak, but every time it lifts its head, the bank seems to shift, as if the river is remembering a name it has not yet spoken.

I sit at the edge of the bank and watch the first cloud pass across the sky. It moves with a sudden decision, as though it were carrying a message written in mist. For a moment I cannot tell whether it is a cloud or a child’s shadow, drifting from the south to claim the sun.

Then the bank begins to move. The stones shift beneath the water’s feet. The crow’s call returns, not from the sky, but from the roots.

The river does not speak. It only arrives.

Before the rain came, the forest was keeping secrets in the hollows of the roots. I sat beneath the old oak and watched the tiny green shoots rise from the dark earth, each one a tiny promise that something would grow. I had always believed that the forest had a way of remembering everything, but today I wondered whether it was remembering me.
